header.subtitle: Present a case so the next person can act: signalment and chief concern, relevant history and objective data, SBAR and veterinary I-PASS handoffs, observation versus interpretation, scope boundaries, closed-loop communication, and PACE escalation — finishing with a two-case presentation lab and a graded assessment.
header.askPrompt: How should a veterinary assistant or technician structure a case presentation using SBAR, and when should they escalate using PACE?
header.resourcesBody: SBAR and I-PASS pocket cards, the closed-loop communication steps, the PACE escalation ladder, the rounds checklist, and your hospital's handoff and documentation standards.
header.resourcesNote: This lesson teaches communication structure only. It does not teach diagnosis, treatment selection, or client-facing diagnostic communication, and it does not replace your hospital's protocols or your state practice act.

overview.heading: Say the right things, in the right order, to the right person — and confirm they landed
overview.intro: A case presentation transfers responsibility for a patient. Handoffs are where safety fails first, and in veterinary hospitals communication failures cluster at shift changes, transfers of case responsibility, and interservice consultations. This lesson gives you a structure for every one of those conversations, a way to separate what you saw from what you think, a clear scope boundary, and a graded escalation ladder for the moments when a patient is changing in front of you.
objectives: Structure a presentation using signalment, chief concern, relevant history, and objective findings, in that order.
Decide what to say now, what to hold ready, and what to leave out.
Prioritize abnormal findings and clinically significant trends over routine data.
Deliver a structured handoff using SBAR, and I-PASS for complex or overnight transfers.
Distinguish an observation from an interpretation and label each explicitly.
Present inside your scope — reporting findings and concerns without naming a diagnosis.
Use closed-loop communication and the PACE ladder to escalate safely.
Deliver a concise presentation and recognize the common mistakes that make one unusable.
overview.connectsForward: Sample Collection taught you to protect the sample; Imaging Support taught you to make the study possible. Case Presentation is what happens to everything you collected and observed: it becomes a report someone else can act on. The SBAR structure, the closed-loop habit, and the PACE ladder carry straight into hospitalized care, anesthesia monitoring, and emergency shifts.

modules.title: Why Presentations Matter & What Goes In Them

modules.content:
A case presentation is not a recital of everything you know about a patient. It is a short, ordered, purposeful transfer of the picture in your head into someone else’s — accurately enough that they can act.

Presenting scope — every module

You do

  • Report signalment, chief concern, history, and objective findings accurately.
  • Prioritize the abnormal findings and trends that changed since the last check.
  • Name your concern — “here is what I see and what worries me.”
  • Close the loop and escalate when the patient no longer matches the plan.

You do not

  • State a diagnosis, or give one to a Pet Parent.
  • Decide or change the treatment plan on your own.
  • Present a guess as if it were an observation.
  • End a handoff before the receiver has acknowledged and accepted it.

In this module you will

  • Explain who a case presentation is for and what it is meant to transfer.
  • Name the four opening elements every presentation needs: signalment, chief concern, relevant history, objective findings.
  • Write a one-liner that orients any listener in a single sentence.
  • Recognize why rushed, unstructured handoffs are a documented patient-safety risk.

Why it matters

Handoffs are where safety fails first

A handoff transfers more than information — it transfers responsibility and authority for the patient, and it is not finished until the receiver understands and accepts it (AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Handoff tool).

In veterinary hospitals, within-team communication failures cluster at exactly these transfer points: shift changes, transfers of case responsibility, and interservice consultations. The Institute of Medicine identified handoffs as a place where safety often fails first (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication).

That is why this is a clinical skill, not a soft skill. The same paper reports that after one hospital implemented SBAR, adverse events fell from 90 to 40 per 1,000 patient-days and adverse drug events fell from 30 to 18 per 1,000 patient-days (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication).

Audience

Decide who you are talking to before you open your mouth

Rounds and presentations should be planned around the audience’s needs — practice-wide rounds where any team member might pick up or transfer a case work differently from ward-specific technician rounds focused on operational handoff (Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice).

The supervising veterinarian

Wants the change since they last looked, your concern in plain words, and what you are asking for. Shortest possible route to a decision.

The oncoming shift

Wants everything they need to keep the patient safe for the next eight hours: what is due, what to watch, and what to do if it happens.

The whole care team

Wants the shared picture — which team member is responsible for the case, what the plan is, and who is updating the Pet Parent (Clinician’s Brief).

Anatomy

The four opening moves, in this order

Every new-patient presentation opens with signalment — species, age, sex and reproductive status, breed — followed by the chief complaint (Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds). SBAR’s “Situation” asks for the same thing: who is speaking, patient identifiers such as age and sex, and a brief statement of the current problem (AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool).

1

Signalment

Species, age, sex and reproductive status, breed, and weight when it matters.

→
2

Chief concern

The reason this patient is in front of you, in the Pet Parent’s or the record’s terms, with a duration.

→
3

Relevant history

A concise, chronological summary — not the whole file (JVME).

→
4

Objective findings

Vitals, exam findings, and results — the abnormal ones first (AHRQ).

The one-liner

One sentence that orients anyone in the room

The published worked example does this in a single breath: “Fluffy Smith, a 5.2 kg, 10-year-old miniature poodle… three-day history of inappetence, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort” (Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice). Build the one-liner first; everything else hangs off it.

Build it

Assemble a one-liner for Fluffy

Three parts, one at a time. Choose the line that belongs in each part. A wrong choice explains itself and lets you try again — nothing is locked.

Part 1 of 3 · Signalment

Part 1 — Who is this patient?

Species, age, sex and reproductive status, breed, and the weight, because it matters for a small dog on insulin.

Part 2 of 3 · Chief concern

Part 2 — Why is she here?

The presenting problem with a duration, in plain language.

Part 3 of 3 · Context

Part 3 — What single piece of context changes everything?

One pertinent chronic condition or current medication that reframes every other finding.

Your presentation so far

Nothing chosen yet. Each line you choose correctly is added here in order, so you can read the whole presentation back at the end.

    Model one-liner: “Fluffy Smith, a 5.2 kg, 10-year-old spayed female miniature poodle, presenting with a three-day history of inappetence, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort, and she has been diabetic for two years on twice-daily insulin.”

    Structure adapted from the worked rounds example in Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice and the signalment-first sequence in Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds.

    Check your thinking

    Four decisions about purpose and audience

    One question at a time. Feedback appears immediately.

    1. Item 1 of 4

      You have finished telling the oncoming technician everything about your patient, and they have not said anything. Is the handoff complete?

    2. Item 2 of 4

      Which opening gives a listener the most usable orientation?

    3. Item 3 of 4

      Where do communication failures most often cause harm in a veterinary hospital?

    4. Item 4 of 4

      Technician-only shift-change rounds in a busy practice typically run how long?

    Purpose first, audience second, structure third. Everything else in this lesson builds on those three.

    Sources for this module+
    • AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Handoff tool
    • Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication
    • Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds
    • Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice
    • AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool

modules.content:
The hardest part of presenting is not remembering things. It is deciding what to leave out — and knowing where the things you leave out have gone, in case you are asked.

Presenting scope — every module

You do

  • Report signalment, chief concern, history, and objective findings accurately.
  • Prioritize the abnormal findings and trends that changed since the last check.
  • Name your concern — “here is what I see and what worries me.”
  • Close the loop and escalate when the patient no longer matches the plan.

You do not

  • State a diagnosis, or give one to a Pet Parent.
  • Decide or change the treatment plan on your own.
  • Present a guess as if it were an observation.
  • End a handoff before the receiver has acknowledged and accepted it.

In this module you will

  • Sort clinical information into what to say now, what to hold ready, and what to leave out.
  • Deliver history as a concise chronological summary rather than a narrative.
  • Lead with abnormal findings and meaningful trends instead of reciting every value.
  • Explain why an over-long handover is a safety problem, not just an efficiency one.

The rule

Concise and chronological beats complete

The rounds-teaching literature is blunt about this: a presentation “will be even better with a concise and chronological summary of the history” (Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds). Pertinent history means the active chronic conditions and current home medications that change how today’s findings read — a diabetic patient’s insulin dose, for example (Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice).

And more is not safer. Overly complicated, long, or detailed handovers may be as much of a patient-safety challenge as handovers without enough detail, if they cause confusion or consume excessive time (Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)).

Today’s patient

Fluffy Smith — hospital day 1

Fluffy SmithPresented for inappetence, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort
  • SpeciesCanine
  • Age10 years
  • SexSpayed female
  • BreedMiniature poodle
  • Weight5.2 kg
  • StatusHospitalized
  • Chief concernThree-day history of inappetence, vomiting, and abdominal discomfort
  • Chronic conditionsDiabetes mellitus, two years, on twice-daily insulin
  • Home medicationsInsulin, twice daily; last dose this morning
  • Temperature101.8 °F — within the expected range
  • Blood glucose300 mg/dL with 0 ketones
  • CBC / chemistryWithin normal limits apart from the expected elevated blood glucose
  • Vaccination statusCurrent
  • MemberPrefers phone updates after 5 p.m.

Case adapted from the published worked rounds example in Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice. Values are illustrative and are used to teach presentation structure, not diagnosis.

Relevance queue

Sort nine pieces of information for a two-minute morning update

Select a line, then choose the lane it belongs in. Everything works with keyboard or touch — there is no dragging. You can move a line as many times as you like before you check.

Say it now

It changes what the listener thinks or does in the next few minutes.

    Have it ready if asked

    Real and relevant, but it does not need airtime unless someone asks.

      Leave it out

      Not relevant to this update. It belongs in the record, not the presentation.

        Trends

        A single value is a data point; three is a story

        Presenters should state the problem list and the meaningful patterns rather than reciting every number, and focus on the most important findings and general concepts rather than exhaustive detail (Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds). Signaling illness severity up front — stable, “watcher”, or unstable — tells the listener how closely to attend before you have said anything else (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication).

        Mabel7-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair — three rechecks over six months
        • SpeciesFeline
        • Age7 years
        • SexSpayed female
        • BreedDomestic shorthair
        • PresentingWeight loss, PU/PD
        • Weight — visit 1, 2, 34.9 kg → 4.6 kg → 4.2 kg
        • BUN / creatinine trendRising at each of the three rechecks
        • Appetite at homeReduced over the past two weeks, per the Pet Parent
        • Temperature today101.2 °F
        • Heart rate today180 bpm, unchanged from prior visits

        Check your thinking

        Three decisions about signal and noise

        One question at a time.

        1. Item 1 of 3

          Which sentence gives the veterinarian the most usable version of Mabel’s data?

        2. Item 2 of 3

          You have eleven normal findings and two abnormal ones. How should the objective section run?

        3. Item 3 of 3

          An overnight technician gives a fifteen-minute, highly detailed handover on a stable patient. What is the risk?

        Relevance is a clinical judgement. When you are unsure, ask yourself what the listener will do differently if they hear it.

        Sources for this module+
        • Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds
        • Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice
        • Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)
        • Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication

modules.title: Structure the Handoff: SBAR & I-PASS

modules.content:
Two structures cover almost everything you will ever need: SBAR for a conversation that needs attention now, and I-PASS for a full transfer of a patient to someone else’s care.

Presenting scope — every module

You do

  • Report signalment, chief concern, history, and objective findings accurately.
  • Prioritize the abnormal findings and trends that changed since the last check.
  • Name your concern — “here is what I see and what worries me.”
  • Close the loop and escalate when the patient no longer matches the plan.

You do not

  • State a diagnosis, or give one to a Pet Parent.
  • Decide or change the treatment plan on your own.
  • Present a guess as if it were an observation.
  • End a handoff before the receiver has acknowledged and accepted it.

In this module you will

  • State the four SBAR components in order and what belongs in each.
  • State the five I-PASS components and when the extra structure is worth it.
  • Assemble an SBAR handoff for a deteriorating patient, one part at a time.
  • Explain why contingency planning and synthesis by the receiver are the parts most often missed.

SBAR

Four components, in order, every time

SBAR frames conversations that need immediate attention and action. Situation opens with the identity of the person communicating, patient identifiers such as age and sex, and a brief statement of the current problem. Background carries the clinical history related to the situation, the signs of the presenting complaint, and test results. Assessment is where you say what you think the problem is, including objective data such as vital signs. Recommendation is what you are asking for (AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool).

S

Situation

Who you are, which patient, and what is happening right now.

“This is Sam on treatment. I’m calling about Rex, the 6-month-old Labrador in run 3.”

B

Background

The history, signs, and results that put the situation in context.

“Admitted overnight for acute bloody diarrhea and lethargy; parvovirus test pending; on IV fluids since 22:00.”

A

Assessment

Your read on it, plus the objective data behind it.

“He’s had four bloody stools since midnight, heart rate is 180, and he is less responsive than at admission. I’m concerned he is deteriorating.”

R

Recommendation

The specific thing you are asking the listener to do.

“Can you come and reassess him now, and tell me whether you want the fluid rate changed?”

I-PASS

When a whole patient is changing hands

For more complex overnight or shift handoffs, veterinary authors recommend I-PASS — Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, and Synthesis by the receiver. It adds the complexity a full transfer needs, especially explicit contingency planning, without becoming unwieldy (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication).

The last letter is the one teams skip. Synthesis by the receiver means they say the plan back to you — and it is the step that turns talking into transferring.

I

Illness severity

One word up front: stable, watcher, or unstable.

“Watcher.”

P

Patient summary

The concise story so far — signalment, problem, course.

“Arthur, 3-year-old neutered male rat terrier, hospital day 2 for vomiting and anorexia with azotemia.”

A

Action list

What is due, when, and who owns it.

“Recheck renal values at 06:00; blood pressure every four hours; weigh him at 08:00.”

S

Situation awareness & contingency

What might happen and exactly what to do if it does.

“If his blood pressure runs high again or he stops urinating, call the clinician on duty right away — don’t wait for the morning.”

S

Synthesis by receiver

The receiver says the plan back and asks questions.

“So: watcher, renal recheck at 06:00, pressures every four hours, and I call you if pressures rise or he stops producing urine.”

The I-PASS example follows the published veterinary worked example (a rat terrier with azotemia and hypertension) described in Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication.

Build it

Rex — a parvovirus suspect handed to the overnight technician

You are calling the veterinarian at 02:10 about a patient who has changed since admission. Assemble the SBAR one part at a time.

Rex6-month-old intact male Labrador retriever — run 3, hospital day 1
  • SpeciesCanine
  • Age6 months
  • SexIntact male
  • BreedLabrador retriever
  • Illness severityWatcher
  • Admitted22:00 for acute bloody diarrhea and lethargy
  • PendingParvovirus test result
  • Since midnightFour bloody stools; most recent 01:55
  • Heart rate180 bpm, up from 140 at admission
  • MentationLess responsive than at admission
  • Current careIV fluids since 22:00; isolation protocol in place

SBAR builder

Assemble the 02:10 call to the veterinarian

Four parts, one at a time. Pick the line that belongs in each SBAR component — wrong choices explain why and let you try again. Your assembled call appears alongside as you go.

Part 1 of 4 · Situation

S — Situation

Who is speaking, which patient, and what is happening right now.

Part 2 of 4 · Background

B — Background

Clinical history related to the situation, the signs, and results.

Part 3 of 4 · Assessment

A — Assessment

What you think is going on, with the objective data behind it. Label the concern as yours.

Part 4 of 4 · Recommendation

R — Recommendation

The specific thing you are asking for. Make it easy to say yes or no to.

Your presentation so far

Nothing chosen yet. Each line you choose correctly is added here in order, so you can read the whole presentation back at the end.

    Model call: “This is Sam on treatment. I’m calling about Rex in run 3, the 6-month-old Labrador — he has deteriorated since admission. He was admitted at 22:00 for acute bloody diarrhea and lethargy, the parvovirus test is still pending, and he has been on IV fluids since admission. He has had four bloody stools since midnight, his heart rate is 180 — up from 140 — and he is less responsive than at admission. I’m concerned he is deteriorating. Can you come and reassess him now, and tell me whether you want the fluid rate changed before then?”

    About thirty seconds, four components, one clear request. Structure per AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool; the deterioration-call framing follows Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF).

    Check your thinking

    Four decisions about structure

    One question at a time.

    1. Item 1 of 4

      Which item belongs in the Situation part of SBAR?

    2. Item 2 of 4

      Which I-PASS element is most often left out of a real handoff?

    3. Item 3 of 4

      When is I-PASS worth the extra structure over plain SBAR?

    4. Item 4 of 4

      What does “synthesis by the receiver” require?

    Structure is not bureaucracy. It is the reason nothing important depends on you remembering it in the moment.

    Sources for this module+
    • AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool
    • Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication
    • Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)
    • AHRQ TeamSTEPPS video page — SBAR on Inpatient Medical Unit

modules.title: Observation vs. Interpretation & Scope
modules.completionHeading: Sort the eight sentences and work through the four vignettes, then select Continue.
modules.completionBody: Selecting Continue records your progress for this module and opens the next module in the lesson.
modules.content:
“Her gums are pale” and “I think she’s anemic” are both useful sentences. They are not the same kind of sentence, and mixing them up is how a guess becomes a fact in someone else’s notes.

Presenting scope — every module

You do

  • Report signalment, chief concern, history, and objective findings accurately.
  • Prioritize the abnormal findings and trends that changed since the last check.
  • Name your concern — “here is what I see and what worries me.”
  • Close the loop and escalate when the patient no longer matches the plan.

You do not

  • State a diagnosis, or give one to a Pet Parent.
  • Decide or change the treatment plan on your own.
  • Present a guess as if it were an observation.
  • End a handoff before the receiver has acknowledged and accepted it.

In this module you will

  • Classify a statement as an objective observation or a clinical interpretation.
  • Voice an interpretation safely by labeling it as your concern.
  • Recognize where the scope boundary sits for assistants and credentialed technicians.
  • Answer a Pet Parent’s diagnostic question without naming a diagnosis.

The distinction

SBAR already draws this line for you

Background carries objective facts — history, signs, test results. Assessment is explicitly where you say what you think the problem is (AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool). The structure itself tells you to label the interpretation as an interpretation.

The risk of blurring the line is documented: unstructured rounding frequently includes extraneous and missing information, and vague call parameters — simply noting that an animal is “outside call parameters” — leave the receiving clinician with no actionable plan and force them to infer intent under pressure (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication).

Observation

Something you saw, measured, counted, or were told. Another person in the room would report it the same way.

Interpretation

What you think it means. Legitimate, valuable — and it must be introduced with words that mark it as yours.

Diagnosis

A clinical conclusion. The veterinarian’s to make and the veterinarian’s to communicate to the client.

Sentence sorter

Observation or interpretation?

Select a sentence, then place it in a lane. Two lanes, eight sentences. Move anything as often as you like before checking.

Observation

Seen, measured, counted, or reported to you.

    Interpretation

    Your read on what the observations mean.

      Say it safely

      The phrasing that keeps an interpretation useful

      Interpretation is not the problem — unlabeled interpretation is. Two small habits fix it: attach the observations that produced your concern, and mark the concern as yours.

      1

      State what you saw

      “Her gums are pale, her heart rate is 160, and her pulses feel weaker than an hour ago.”

      →
      2

      Name the concern as yours

      “I’m concerned she may be losing blood.”

      →
      3

      Ask for something

      “Can you reassess her now?”

      Scope

      Report and raise; do not diagnose or decide

      Scope of practice — which tasks a credentialed technician or nurse versus an assistant may perform, and under what supervision — is poorly defined or absent in many U.S. jurisdictions. NAVTA’s scope-of-practice report calls for itemized, dual-list task frameworks and standardized supervision levels specifically to protect patient safety and clarify delegation (NAVTA — Scope of Practice Report).

      Working to the top of your legal scope is a professional expectation, not overreach: AAHA’s utilization guidelines note that under-utilizing credentialed technicians relative to their training is a leading driver of attrition (2023 AAHA Technician Utilization Guidelines). Confident, bounded reporting is the skill — “here is what I see and what concerns me”, never “here is the diagnosis”.

      Your hospital’s policy and your state’s practice act set the actual boundary. When the two disagree with a colleague’s expectations, the policy wins and the question goes to the veterinarian.

      Scope vignettes

      Four conversations, four scope-appropriate answers

      One question at a time. Each has a phrasing that stays inside scope.

      1. Vignette 1 of 4

        A worried Pet Parent in the lobby asks you: “Is it pyometra?” What do you say?

      2. Vignette 2 of 4

        You are convinced a hospitalized dog is bleeding internally. What is the in-scope way to raise it with the veterinarian?

      3. Vignette 3 of 4

        A colleague asks you to record “patient is stable” on a chart when you have not assessed the patient yourself.

      4. Vignette 4 of 4

        You are a veterinary assistant and the credentialed technician is busy. A task you have never been trained on needs doing before rounds.

      Report clearly, concern openly, decide never. That is the whole boundary.

      Sources for this module+
      • AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool
      • Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication
      • NAVTA — Scope of Practice Report
      • 2023 AAHA Technician Utilization Guidelines

modules.title: Closed-Loop Communication & PACE Escalation

modules.content:
Speaking is not communicating. A message only counts when it comes back to you — and when the patient is changing in front of you, how you escalate matters as much as what you say.

Presenting scope — every module

You do

  • Report signalment, chief concern, history, and objective findings accurately.
  • Prioritize the abnormal findings and trends that changed since the last check.
  • Name your concern — “here is what I see and what worries me.”
  • Close the loop and escalate when the patient no longer matches the plan.

You do not

  • State a diagnosis, or give one to a Pet Parent.
  • Decide or change the treatment plan on your own.
  • Present a guess as if it were an observation.
  • End a handoff before the receiver has acknowledged and accepted it.

In this module you will

  • Perform the four steps of closed-loop communication in order.
  • Use teach-back and read-back to confirm a message was received as intended.
  • Climb the PACE ladder — Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency — one rung at a time.
  • Explain why psychological safety determines whether escalation happens at all.

Closed-loop communication

Four steps, and the loop is not closed until the fourth

Closed-loop communication requires specifying who is being addressed, specifying which patient, having the receiver repeat back the message, and having the sender verify that the repeat-back was accurate (Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)). AHRQ frames the same requirement for handoffs: responsibility cannot be relinquished until the receiver acknowledges that the handoff is understood and accepted (AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Handoff tool).

Close the loop

Place the four steps in order

Select the step you believe comes next. If it is not next, you will be told why and can try again. Nothing is locked and you can reset at any time.

    All four steps placed. Notice that steps three and four are the ones under time pressure — and they are the two that actually transfer the message.

    Teach-back

    The same idea, pointed at understanding rather than accuracy

    A read-back confirms the words. Teach-back confirms the meaning: you ask the receiver to say the plan back in their own words. In a handoff, that is exactly what I-PASS calls synthesis by the receiver (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication), and it is why a receiver who says nothing has not accepted anything.

    PACE

    Graded assertiveness when something is unsafe

    PACE — Probe, Alert, Challenge, Emergency — is a graded assertiveness tool for speaking up. The published veterinary illustration walks up the ladder during a difficult endotracheal intubation: “Do you realize the ETCO2 trace is poor?”, then “I’m concerned the tube is not correctly in place”, then “If we don’t correct this now, our patient is going to become hypoxic”, and finally “STOP — this is an emergency!” (Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)).

    You start low and climb only as far as you need to. Starting at the top for a minor concern costs you credibility; staying at the bottom when a patient is deteriorating costs the patient.

    Otis9-year-old neutered male domestic shorthair — under anesthesia for a dental procedure
    • SpeciesFeline
    • Age9 years
    • SexNeutered male
    • ProcedureDental
    • Illness severityUnstable
    • CapnographyETCO2 trace has become poor over the last two minutes
    • Pulse oximetrySpO2 falling
    • Chest movementLess than expected for the set tidal volume
    • AnesthetistFocused on the surgical site, has not looked at the monitor

    PACE ladder

    Climb the ladder for Otis, one rung at a time

    Each rung shows the situation as it stands. Choose the phrasing that matches that rung — not the one that feels most dramatic. Choosing wrong explains the level you actually used and lets you try again.

    • PProbeAsk a question that makes the other person look at what you are seeing.
    • AAlertName your concern and suggest a course of action.
    • CChallengeState the consequence plainly and require a response.
    • EEmergencyStop the activity. Use your authority as a team member to protect the patient.

    Rung 1 of 4

    Rung 1 — Probe

    You have been watching the monitor. The trace has changed in the last thirty seconds and the anesthetist is looking at the mouth.

    Rung 2 of 4

    Rung 2 — Alert

    The anesthetist glanced at the monitor and carried on. The trace has not improved and the saturation is dropping.

    Rung 3 of 4

    Rung 3 — Challenge

    Thirty more seconds have passed. Nothing has been checked.

    Rung 4 of 4

    Rung 4 — Emergency

    The saturation has continued to fall and the patient’s status has changed in front of you.

    You climbed all four rungs. In a real event you may reach rung four in seconds — the ladder is about pitching each statement correctly, not about waiting.

    Why people do not speak up

    Psychological safety is the precondition

    Escalation and speak-up behavior depend on psychological safety: team members at every level, including students, assistants, and technicians, have to feel safe asking questions, raising concerns, and reporting mistakes. Low psychological safety is linked to staff being less likely to flag potential errors (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication; Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)).

    Two behaviors degrade it fast. Condescension and second-guessing between services discourage future consultation and are a form of hindsight bias (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication). Incivility — eye-rolling, ignoring, belittling — measurably degrades team performance and safety (Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)). If you receive a presentation, how you receive it determines what you are told next time.

    Check your thinking

    Three decisions about closing loops

    One question at a time.

    1. Item 1 of 3

      A veterinarian gives you a verbal instruction across a busy treatment area. What do you do first?

    2. Item 2 of 3

      You escalate a concern and the response is an eye-roll. What is the patient-safety consequence?

    3. Item 3 of 3

      Which of these is a properly closed loop?

    If you did not hear it come back, it did not go out.

    Sources for this module+
    • Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)
    • AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Handoff tool
    • Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication

modules.content:
Two patients, two very different presentations. One is a thirty-second urgent report; the other is a calm recheck update. Same structure, different weight.

Presenting scope — every module

You do

  • Report signalment, chief concern, history, and objective findings accurately.
  • Prioritize the abnormal findings and trends that changed since the last check.
  • Name your concern — “here is what I see and what worries me.”
  • Close the loop and escalate when the patient no longer matches the plan.

You do not

  • State a diagnosis, or give one to a Pet Parent.
  • Decide or change the treatment plan on your own.
  • Present a guess as if it were an observation.
  • End a handoff before the receiver has acknowledged and accepted it.

In this module you will

  • Assemble a complete presentation for an urgent patient without naming a diagnosis.
  • Assemble a recheck update that leads with a trend rather than a single value.
  • Judge your own delivery for length — optionally against a clock.
  • Recognize the common mistakes that make a presentation unusable.

Watch first

A modeled case presentation — Mabel

Before you build anything, watch the presentation you are about to practice. A PetNurse presents Mabel — the same 7-year-old domestic shorthair recheck patient you met in Module 2 — to the veterinarian, who acknowledges the message, gives a next action, and receives a read-back.

Listen for four things: the signalment and visit context that open the presentation; the single sentence that compresses three visits of data into a direction of travel; the concern stated as the presenter’s own, with a specific request; and the closed loop at the end, where the veterinarian summarizes what they heard and the PetNurse reads the plan back. Notice what is not there: no diagnosis, no treatment decision, and no recital of normal values.

Read the full transcript+

Full spoken script of the demonstration, in order. Speaker labels are shown for every turn.

Narrator

A strong case presentation is not a recital of the entire chart. It is a concise transfer of the patient picture, organized so the veterinarian can quickly understand what matters and decide what happens next.

In this demonstration, a PetNurse presents Mabel, a stable feline recheck patient. Listen for four elements: who the patient is, why she is here, the meaningful trend, and a clear concern with a specific request.

PetNurse

Mabel is a seven-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair, here for her third recheck, being monitored for progressive weight loss with increased drinking and urination.

She has lost zero point seven kilograms across three rechecks in six months, and her B U N and creatinine have risen at every one. The Pet Parent also reports her appetite has dropped over the past two weeks. Everything else today is unchanged.

I’m concerned the trend is continuing. Do you want anything added before she goes home?

Veterinarian

I heard a stable recheck patient with continued weight loss, rising renal values, and a new decrease in appetite.

Yes. Please keep Mabel with us while I review the results and examine her. I will update you after I speak with her Pet Parent.

PetNurse

Keep Mabel with us for now, and wait for your update after the examination and Pet Parent conversation. Understood.

Narrator

Notice why that presentation was usable.

First, signalment and visit context identified the patient and the purpose.

Second, three visits became one meaningful trend: Mabel’s weight fell while B U N and creatinine continued to rise.

Third, the PetNurse added the new Pet Parent-reported change, reduced appetite, and summarized the other findings as unchanged.

Finally, she stayed within scope. She did not name a diagnosis or choose treatment. She stated her concern and asked for the next action.

The veterinarian acknowledged the message, summarized the concerns, gave a clear direction, and named who would update the Pet Parent. The PetNurse closed the loop with a read-back.

Help the listener answer four questions: Who is this patient? Why are we talking now? What changed? What do you need from me?

Be accurate. Be concise. Lead with the pattern, state your concern, and close the loop.

Now do it yourself

The two labs below ask you to assemble presentations from scratch — an urgent one and a recheck one. The video is a model, not a script to memorize: your wording will differ, but the four elements and the closed loop should not.

Lab 1

Juno — acute abdominal distension, five minutes after arrival

You are the first person to see this patient. The veterinarian is finishing a consultation two rooms away. This presentation has to be short, factual, and urgent — and it must not name a condition.

Juno4-year-old spayed female German shepherd — walk-in, 5 minutes ago
  • SpeciesCanine
  • Age4 years
  • SexSpayed female
  • BreedGerman shepherd
  • Illness severityUnstable
  • Chief concernSudden abdominal distension and repeated non-productive retching for one hour
  • Mucous membranesPale, capillary refill time slightly prolonged
  • Heart rate160 bpm
  • BehaviorRestless, unable to settle, pacing
  • History from Pet ParentAte a large meal and then ran in the yard
  • Preventive careVaccinations current; no chronic medications

Lab 1

Build the urgent presentation for Juno

Five parts, one at a time. This one is timed only if you want it to be — the optional timer appears once you finish, and it never blocks anything.

Part 1 of 5 · Signalment

Part 1 — Signalment

Enough for the listener to picture the patient, no more.

Part 2 of 5 · Chief concern

Part 2 — Chief concern and urgency

What is happening, for how long, and how sick the patient looks.

Part 3 of 5 · Objective

Part 3 — Objective findings, abnormal first

Lead with what is abnormal. Compress the normal findings.

Part 4 of 5 · Concern

Part 4 — Your concern, labeled as yours

This is the assessment layer. Mark it as your read, not as fact.

Part 5 of 5 · Request

Part 5 — The request

One specific ask, with a timeframe.

Your presentation so far

Nothing chosen yet. Each line you choose correctly is added here in order, so you can read the whole presentation back at the end.

    Model presentation (about twenty-five seconds): “Juno, a 4-year-old spayed female German shepherd, arrived five minutes ago with one hour of sudden abdominal distension and repeated non-productive retching — she looks unstable to me. Her mucous membranes are pale with a slightly prolonged capillary refill time, heart rate 160, and she is restless and cannot settle. I’m concerned about her perfusion and how quickly this came on. Can you assess her now? I’ll stay with her and have the team ready.”

    Note what is absent: no condition is named, nothing is decided, and no normal finding is recited. Structure per Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds and AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool; scope framing per NAVTA — Scope of Practice Report.

    Optional 60-second delivery timer

    Entirely optional. Nothing in this module is gated on it, and you can stop it at any time. Assemble your presentation first, then read it aloud once against the clock if you want to test how it sounds under time pressure.

    Lab 2

    Mabel — a recheck where the trend is the finding

    Same structure, completely different tempo. Nothing here is urgent; the skill is making three visits’ worth of data land in two sentences.

    Mabel7-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair — third recheck
    • SpeciesFeline
    • Age7 years
    • SexSpayed female
    • BreedDomestic shorthair
    • Illness severityStable
    • Chief concernProgressive weight loss with increased drinking and urination
    • Weight trend4.9 kg → 4.6 kg → 4.2 kg over six months
    • BUN / creatinineRisen at each of the three rechecks
    • Pet Parent reportAppetite reduced over the past two weeks
    • Temperature and heart rate todayUnchanged from prior visits
    • HandlingTolerates restraint well; no handling precautions

    Lab 2

    Build the recheck update for Mabel

    Four parts. The winning move in this one is compression — three visits of data belong in a single sentence about direction.

    Part 1 of 4 · Signalment

    Part 1 — Signalment and visit context

    Who she is and why she is here today.

    Part 2 of 4 · Chief concern

    Part 2 — The presenting problem

    The reason for the recheck series, in observable terms.

    Part 3 of 4 · Trend

    Part 3 — The trend, in one sentence

    Three visits of data. One sentence about direction.

    Part 4 of 4 · Concern & request

    Part 4 — Your concern and what you are asking

    Add the new Pet Parent-reported change, label your concern, and make one ask.

    Your presentation so far

    Nothing chosen yet. Each line you choose correctly is added here in order, so you can read the whole presentation back at the end.

      Model presentation (about twenty seconds): “Mabel, a 7-year-old spayed female domestic shorthair, here for her third recheck, being monitored for progressive weight loss with increased drinking and urination. She has lost 0.7 kg across three rechecks in six months and her BUN and creatinine have risen at every one. The Pet Parent also reports her appetite has dropped over the past two weeks. Everything else today is unchanged. I’m concerned the trend is continuing — do you want anything added before she goes home?”

      Trend-first structure per Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds; the “otherwise unchanged” compression per Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice.

      Optional 60-second delivery timer

      Entirely optional. Nothing in this module is gated on it, and you can stop it at any time. Assemble your presentation first, then read it aloud once against the clock if you want to test how it sounds under time pressure.

      Before you finish

      The mistakes that make a presentation unusable

      Every item below is documented in the sources for this lesson. Most of them are habits, not knowledge gaps.

      Missing or extraneous information

      Unstructured rounding routinely contains both at once, along with absent situation awareness and contingency planning (JAVMA).

      Uninformative call parameters

      “Outside call parameters” with no contingency plan forces the clinician to improvise under uncertainty (JAVMA).

      Skipping the problem list

      Jumping straight to diagnostics and plan without framing the key issues first (JVME).

      Rambling, non-chronological history

      A concise chronological summary is the standard (JVME).

      No acknowledgment or read-back

      The sender never confirms the message landed, so responsibility never actually transfers (AHRQ; TVP).

      No team member assigned responsibility for the case

      Failing to state which team member is responsible going forward and who will update the Pet Parent (Clinician’s Brief; AHRQ).

      Documentation

      Say it, then write it

      Effective handoffs pair the verbal presentation with a written record — formal handoff systems should have both written and verbal components (Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication). Recording rounds answers on the practice census keeps receptionists, technicians, veterinarians, and clients aligned, and when a case moves between services, confirm that the chart has been passed along with all workups (Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice). Electronic handoffs work best when reinforced by direct verbal communication, not as a replacement for it (AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Handoff tool).

      Sources & framework credits

      Everything this lesson is built on

      Frameworks used in this lesson

      • SBAR — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — SBAR tool
      • Handoff principles — transfer of responsibility, acknowledgment, and the opportunity to ask questions. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS — Handoff tool
      • I-PASS and the veterinary within-team communication evidence, including the SBAR adverse-event reduction figures and the worked I-PASS example. Cummings et al., JAVMA 260(6), 2022 — Improving within-team communication
      • Closed-loop communication and the PACE graded-assertiveness ladder, plus the incivility and handover-length evidence. Today’s Veterinary Practice, 2024 — How In-Clinic Communication Affects Patient Safety (PDF)
      • Case-presentation content and order, the problem list, and common presentation mistakes. Lane & Cornell, JVME, 2013 — Making the Most of Hospital Rounds
      • Rounds structure, the worked “Fluffy” example, pertinent history, and the 10–15 minute technician rounds benchmark. Clinician’s Brief, 2014 — Rounds: Ensuring They Work for the Patient & the Practice
      • Scope of practice for credentialed technicians, nurses, and assistants. NAVTA — Scope of Practice Report
      • Technician utilization and working to the top of license. 2023 AAHA Technician Utilization Guidelines
      • Video — TeamSTEPPS: SBAR on Inpatient Medical Unit, AHRQ Patient Safety. AHRQ TeamSTEPPS video page — SBAR on Inpatient Medical Unit

      All patients in this lesson are teaching cases. Arthur, Fluffy, and the ETCO2 escalation are adapted from the published worked examples in the sources above; Rex, Mabel, and Juno are composites written for this lesson. Numbers are illustrative and are used to teach presentation structure — they are not clinical reference ranges, and nothing here replaces your hospital’s protocols, your state practice act, or veterinarian direction.

modules.title: Final Assessment
modules.content:
Twelve questions covering the whole lesson. One question at a time, immediate feedback, and a pass mark of 80 percent. You can retake it as many times as you need.

Presenting scope — every module

You do

  • Report signalment, chief concern, history, and objective findings accurately.
  • Prioritize the abnormal findings and trends that changed since the last check.
  • Name your concern — “here is what I see and what worries me.”
  • Close the loop and escalate when the patient no longer matches the plan.

You do not

  • State a diagnosis, or give one to a Pet Parent.
  • Decide or change the treatment plan on your own.
  • Present a guess as if it were an observation.
  • End a handoff before the receiver has acknowledged and accepted it.

Before you begin

How this assessment works

Questions appear one at a time with a progress indicator. Feedback appears the moment you answer, and you can move back through questions you have already answered.

Your score is shown after the final question. 80% or higher — that is 10 of 12 — marks this assessment and the Case Presentation lesson complete. If you score below that, use Retake assessment, and revisit any module from the curriculum first.

What is being tested

Communication judgement, not diagnosis. Every correct answer is something an assistant or technician says, structures, confirms, or escalates. Nothing in this assessment asks you to name a condition or choose a treatment.

quiz.q: Part 1 · StructureWhat are the four components of SBAR, in order?
opts: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
Signalment, Background, Assessment, Response
Summary, Baseline, Action, Review
Situation, Baseline, Analysis, Request
quiz.exp: SBAR is Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation — the AHRQ TeamSTEPPS structure for a conversation that needs immediate attention and action.

quiz.q: Part 1 · StructureWhich of these belongs in the Situation part of an SBAR handoff?
opts: The six-month laboratory trend
Who you are, which patient, and a brief statement of the current problem
The change you want made to the fluid rate
The Member’s preferred call-back time
quiz.exp: Situation opens with the identity of the person communicating, patient identifiers such as age and sex, and a brief statement of the current problem. The lab trend is Background; the fluid change is Recommendation.

quiz.q: Part 1 · StructurePut these case-presentation elements in the correct order.
opts: Chief concern → signalment → objective exam findings → relevant history
Signalment → chief concern → relevant history → objective exam findings
Objective exam findings → signalment → chief concern → relevant history
Relevant history → chief concern → signalment → objective exam findings
quiz.exp: Signalment first, then the chief concern, then a concise chronological history, then the objective findings. That is the sequence the veterinary rounds-teaching literature sets out.

quiz.q: Part 1 · StructureWhat are the five components of I-PASS?
opts: Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis by receiver
Identity, Problem, Assessment, Signalment, Summary
Introduction, Plan, Assessment, Status, Signature
Illness severity, Prognosis, Action list, Schedule, Summary
quiz.exp: I-PASS is Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, and Synthesis by the receiver. Veterinary authors recommend it for complex or overnight handoffs.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Observation and interpretationA technician says: “His gums are pale and his heart rate is 160.” What kind of statement is that?
opts: An interpretation
An observation
A diagnosis
A recommendation
quiz.exp: Both parts are things that were seen or measured, so it is an observation. Objective data of this kind is what SBAR asks you to bring to the Assessment component.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Observation and interpretationA technician says: “I think he’s anemic and might be bleeding internally.” Which description is correct?
opts: An observation, and it should be recorded as a finding
An interpretation, and it should never be voiced
An interpretation, and it is appropriate to raise with the veterinarian as a labeled concern — but not to present to a Pet Parent as a diagnosis
A diagnosis, and it is within a technician’s scope to state
quiz.exp: It is an interpretation. Raising it with the veterinarian as your concern, supported by the observations behind it, is exactly what a technician should do. Naming a condition to a client is the veterinarian’s role.

quiz.q: Part 2 · Observation and interpretationA worried Pet Parent asks a veterinary assistant, “Is it pyometra?” What is the scope-appropriate response?
opts: Confirm it, since the record already says so
Report the signs that have been observed and route the diagnostic question to the veterinarian
Say that you are not permitted to discuss the patient
Give the most likely diagnosis but add that it is unconfirmed
quiz.exp: Report the observed signs and the next step, and hand the diagnostic question to the veterinarian. Scope-of-practice guidance puts naming a diagnosis outside an assistant’s role — and hedged phrasing does not change that.

quiz.q: Part 3 · Relevance and common mistakesA cat has three rechecks with a rising creatinine and steady weight loss. What is the most useful way to present this?
opts: Read every value from all three visits in order
Report only today’s creatinine, because it is the most recent
State the direction of travel across the three rechecks in one sentence
Hand over the printed results and let the veterinarian read them
quiz.exp: The trend is the finding. Presenters are advised to highlight the meaningful patterns and the problem list rather than reciting every data point.

quiz.q: Part 3 · Relevance and common mistakesWhich of these is a documented common mistake in case presentations?
opts: Stating the problem list before the diagnostic plan
Skipping the problem list and jumping straight to the diagnostic plan
Giving a concise chronological history
Naming who will update the client
quiz.exp: Skipping the problem list and moving straight to diagnostics and plan is the documented error. The other three options are all good practice.

quiz.q: Part 3 · Relevance and common mistakesAn overnight handover is very long and highly detailed for a stable patient. How should that be viewed?
opts: Always safer, because nothing can be missed
A potential patient-safety problem in itself, if it causes confusion or consumes excessive time
Acceptable only for surgical patients
A documentation issue rather than a communication issue
quiz.exp: Overly complicated, long, or detailed handovers may be as much of a patient-safety challenge as handovers without enough detail. Brevity is a safety feature, not just an efficiency one.

quiz.q: Part 4 · Closing the loop and escalatingWhat are the four steps of closed-loop communication?
opts: Specify who is being addressed → specify which patient → receiver repeats the message back → sender verifies the repeat-back was accurate
Write the order → perform the order → sign the record → tell the client
Ask → answer → document → file
State the concern → escalate → document → debrief
quiz.exp: Name the person, name the patient, have the receiver call it back, and verify the call-back. Without the last two steps you have spoken but not communicated.

quiz.q: Part 4 · Closing the loop and escalatingDuring anesthesia you notice the ETCO2 trace is poor and nobody else has reacted. Using PACE, what do you say first?
opts: “STOP — this is an emergency!”
“If we don’t correct this now, our patient is going to become hypoxic.”
“Do you realize the ETCO2 trace is poor?”
Nothing — wait to see whether it improves
quiz.exp: Start at Probe: a question that redirects attention. Alert, Challenge, and Emergency follow only if the situation does not resolve. Saying nothing is the failure PACE exists to prevent.
